title: Brain and Visual Perception: The Story of a 25-Year Collaboration
author: David H. Hubel; Torsten N. Wiesel
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. H3 was explicitly examined because most pages reprint research papers. The annotated chronological structure, extensive accounts of experimental decisions, autobiographies and retrospective corrections make the main purpose a history and explanation of discovery, rather than specialist training or a lookup reference. Zeki and Martinez-Conde support this reading. Technical detail remains substantial; eligibility confidence moderate. Scientific-biography exception applies to V3. Visual mechanisms, not disease or US social history, dominate; T11=T12=0. No serious veto established. Reader praise is strong but based on only 12 ratings.
notes: Original experimental evidence and retrospective discussion expose methods and mistakes; authors' selection and dated models remain limits.
Integrates cells, circuits, development and scientific organization, with little industry or institutional economics.
Strong lessons in experimental design, collaboration and following anomalous observations.
Interventions and recordings connect neural responses to visual mechanisms, with explicit experimental chains.

D=8, moderate confidence from Zeki's extended review, Martinez-Conde's review and contents. Separate experiments add constraints and revisions. Reprinted articles carry technical detail beyond many readers' needs; full-text coverage was not audited.
A durable record of scientific discovery, not a current neuroscience survey.
Scientific method and information processing fit well; direct industrial application is limited.
Primary investigators with Nobel recognition and substantial specialist scrutiny.
Chronological papers and surrounding commentary show cumulative discovery; long papers interrupt narrative flow.
Specialist reviewers praise disciplined, readable exposition.

title: The Other Side of History: Daily Life in the Ancient World
author: Robert Garland
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. A published 379-page course guidebook is documented, so the nomination is not discarded merely because the source consumed lectures. This is explanatory social history, not technical training. Lives of marginalized groups, slavery, disability and social conditions are major organizing subjects; T11=-10. Daily life rather than political doctrine or military strategy dominates, T12=0. Broad ancient-to-medieval coverage ends approximately 1500; H13 reaches its -12 cap. Food, labor, status and material constraints supply transferable content; V3 is not established. Religion is treated historically, not as doctrine to defend. Reader rating covers the course, not an independently rated print edition.
notes: Specialist synthesis draws on historical sources, but imaginative reconstruction and uneven ancient evidence limit certainty.
Connects material subsistence, labor, social status and institutions across several societies.
Some useful comparisons of constraints, with limited direct decision utility.
Explains how conditions shape daily routines; many sections describe rather than test causes.

D=7, moderate confidence from the lecture outline, Roth's discussion citing the guidebook and reader reports. Different societies add substantive comparisons; ordinary-life detail has variable relevance. No paragraph-level guidebook audit.
Ancient social conditions remain durable historical knowledge.
Limited technology, trade and civilization fit; desired industrial mechanisms are peripheral.
Classics scholar with relevant historical expertise.
Accessible thematic perspectives; episodic structure can limit cumulative argument.
Generally clear exposition; imagined viewpoints need qualification.
